name: The 1979 Revolution
description: The Iranian Revolution brought down Mohammad Reza Pahlavi’s monarchy in 1979 and opened a struggle over the country’s political future. Ruhollah Khomeini emerged as the dominant revolutionary leader, while the new Islamic Republic institutionalized clerical authority alongside elected institutions. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: The 1979 Iranian Revolution | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: How demonstrations and political crisis ended Iran’s monarchy, brought Khomeini back from exile, and opened the struggle to establish the Islamic Republic.

content.heading: A revolution across several cities
content.content:
The revolution was a developing confrontation across Iran rather than a single uprising in Tehran. In January 1978, an insulting newspaper article about Ruhollah Khomeini, a Shi‘i cleric living in exile, helped trigger demonstrations in Qom, an important religious center. Repression and mourning generated further mobilization, including demonstrations in Tabriz. Religious commemorations supplied occasions for renewed protest, connecting local grievances to a national confrontation with the monarchy. [s1]

The geography matters: Qom’s religious networks, Tabriz’s demonstrations, and Tehran’s increasingly direct confrontation with the state belonged to the same escalating crisis. Accounts disagree sharply about some casualty totals. Those disagreements should not obscure the documented role of state violence in sustaining opposition, but they make precise death counts unsuitable without further source comparison. [s1][s2]

content.heading: From political crisis to the monarchy’s collapse
content.content:
During 1978, demonstrations, changes of government, and repression failed to restore the shah’s authority. The shooting of demonstrators in Tehran’s Jaleh Square on 8 September became known as Black Friday. Later that year, Khomeini moved from Iraq to France, where greater access to international media strengthened his ability to address events in Iran. [s2]

The shah left Iran on 16 January 1979. His departure did not immediately settle who governed: Shapour Bakhtiar remained prime minister, while Khomeini rejected his administration’s legitimacy. Khomeini returned to Tehran on 1 February. Fighting and the withdrawal of military support from Bakhtiar brought the monarchy’s remaining governing structure down in February. These were successive steps in a breakdown of authority, rather than an orderly transfer between governments. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Overthrow did not settle the new order
content.content:
Mehdi Bazargan, associated with the Freedom Movement, headed a provisional government appointed by Khomeini. Their differences exposed a central unresolved question: would religious leadership guide a government, or exercise governing authority itself? Bazargan did not endorse Khomeini’s principle of velayat-e faqih, usually translated as guardianship of the Islamic jurist. His later account distinguished the overthrow of the shah from subsequent developments that he believed contradicted the revolution’s original aims. [s1]

The constitutional settlement established an Islamic Republic with elections and a powerful religious leadership. The constitution’s own account presents this outcome as the fulfillment of the revolution; that is the state’s foundational interpretation, rather than evidence that all opponents of the monarchy wanted the same political system. The text available here incorporates amendments made in 1989 and must not be read as an unchanged copy of the original settlement. [s3]

Understanding the revolution therefore requires separating two questions: how the monarchy lost power, and how one conception of revolutionary government became institutionally dominant. [s1][s3]

content.title: Selected steps in the revolutionary transition
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["January 1978: protests in Qom"] -->|"Followed by further mobilization"| B["February 1978: demonstrations in Tabriz"]
  B -->|"Escalating national crisis"| C["September 1978: Black Friday in Tehran"]
  C -->|"Political crisis continues"| D["16 January 1979: shah leaves Iran"]
  D -->|"Return from exile"| E["1 February 1979: Khomeini returns"]
  E -->|"Fighting and loss of military support for Bakhtiar"| F["February 1979: monarchy collapses"]
```
content.summary: The arrows show chronological succession and explicitly described developments. They do not claim that any single event was sufficient to cause the revolution.

name: Iran–Iraq War
description: The Iran–Iraq War began with Iraq’s invasion of Iran in September 1980 and continued until a ceasefire took effect in August 1988. Iranian counteroffensives, subsequent fighting inside Iraq, chemical warfare, and prolonged diplomacy made it a defining conflict for both countries. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: The Iran–Iraq War, 1980–1988 | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An introduction to Iraq’s invasion, Iran’s counteroffensives, chemical warfare, and the UN process that produced the August 1988 ceasefire.

content.heading: An invasion and a contested frontier
content.content:
Iraq began the war on 22 September 1980 with air attacks and a ground invasion of Iran. A central geographical issue was the Shatt al-Arab, known in Iran as the Arvand Rud, the waterway along part of the countries’ southern frontier. The conflict also developed in the unsettled regional circumstances following Iran’s revolution. Border disputes and political antagonism help explain the confrontation, but do not make the decision to invade an impersonal or inevitable event. [s1]

Khuzestan, Iran’s southwestern province, became a principal battlefield. The experience of its inhabitants cannot be reduced to a simple division between Arabs and Persians: the scholarly account consulted here records that Iranian Arabs did not rise in support of the invading Iraqi forces as Saddam Hussein had anticipated. [s1]

content.heading: Recovery of territory and continuation of war
content.content:
Iran’s recovery of Khorramshahr in May 1982 marked a major reversal of the invasion. Later that year, Iranian forces advanced into Iraq. This distinction is essential: repelling an invasion and continuing a war across the international frontier were different strategic phases. Iranian leaders debated the feasibility and costs of an offensive, while their conditions for a settlement went beyond a simple halt to fighting. [s1]

The change in battlefield position did not produce agreement on peace. The United Nations’ subsequent diplomatic record shows how a conflict can continue even when proposals for ending it already exist: ceasefire terms require acceptance, implementation arrangements, and confidence that the other party will comply. [s2]

content.heading: Chemical warfare and the international response
content.content:
Chemical weapons were a documented feature of the conflict. In Resolution 612, adopted on 9 May 1988, the UN Security Council condemned their continued use as contrary to the Geneva Protocol. It also called for strict controls on exports of chemicals suitable for producing chemical weapons. The resolution establishes an international response to prohibited warfare; its language should not be stretched into an incident-by-incident attribution or a complete accounting of victims. [s3]

That distinction matters when reading diplomatic documents. A resolution can condemn conduct and demand preventive measures without supplying the medical evidence, perpetrator findings, or comprehensive casualty figures needed for a detailed history of individual attacks. [s3]

content.heading: Ending the fighting required a separate process
content.content:
Security Council Resolution 598 was adopted on 20 July 1987, but the ceasefire took effect on 20 August 1988. These dates describe different developments and should not be treated as interchangeable endpoints. The United Nations Iran–Iraq Military Observer Group, or UNIIMOG, was established to verify and supervise the cessation of hostilities and withdrawal toward the internationally recognized boundary. [s2]

Withdrawal remained a separate implementation problem after the guns fell silent. The UN account describes forces still requiring adjustment around the border during the later monitoring period. The useful conclusion is therefore more precise than saying that a resolution ended the war: diplomacy produced a framework, the parties accepted a ceasefire, and observers then monitored practical compliance. [s2]

content.title: From a Security Council framework to monitored implementation
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["20 July 1987: Resolution 598 adopted"] -->|"Framework for a negotiated end to fighting"| B["Parties agree to ceasefire arrangements"]
  B -->|"Observer mission established"| C["9 August 1988: Resolution 619 establishes UNIIMOG"]
  C -->|"Observers deployed for monitoring"| D["20 August 1988: ceasefire takes effect"]
  D -->|"Verification and supervision"| E["Ceasefire and border withdrawal monitored"]
```
content.summary: Adopting a diplomatic framework, commencing a ceasefire, and verifying withdrawal were distinct steps. UNIIMOG monitored implementation; it did not itself negotiate away every underlying dispute.

name: Political Developments after 1979
description: Politics after the 1979 revolution has involved recurring conflict over elected authority, religious leadership, political participation, and civil rights. Constitutional arrangements explain part of this history, while protest movements, repression, and wartime leadership changes reveal developments beyond the formal text. [s1][s2][s5]

seo.title: Iran’s Political Developments after 1979 | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: A sourced introduction to constitutional authority, protest movements, civil rights, and recent political upheaval, with explicit research gaps.

content.heading: Elections within a wider structure of authority
content.content:
The Islamic Republic’s constitutional structure combines elected institutions with religious leadership and supervisory bodies. In the consolidated constitution incorporating the 1989 amendments, the president heads the executive except in matters assigned directly to the Leader. The Leader holds supreme military command and important appointment powers. The Guardian Council reviews legislation for compatibility with Islam and the constitution and supervises specified elections. These provisions establish formal authority; they do not measure how independently institutions operate in practice. [s1]

This distinction helps explain why a presidential election cannot, by itself, describe the distribution of power across the state. It also guards against treating constitutional promises as proof of their implementation. [s1]

content.heading: Successive movements challenged different limits
content.content:
The Green Movement developed after the disputed presidential election of 2009. Later demonstrations had different immediate triggers: protests beginning in Mashhad in December 2017 focused initially on economic conditions, while the November 2019 protests followed a fuel-price increase. These episodes should not be flattened into one continuous movement with identical participants or demands. Their differing starting points show how disputes over representation and material conditions could both become confrontations with political authority. [s2][s3]

In 2022, the death of Mahsa Jina Amini following her detention by the morality police triggered the Woman, Life, Freedom protests. An Associated Press account of the UN fact-finding mission’s 2024 findings reported that the mission attributed her death to physical violence and found crimes against humanity in the response to protests. These are attributed investigative findings, rather than a claim that every allegation has received a judicial determination. [s4]

content.heading: Changes in office and limits on dissent
content.content:
President Ebrahim Raisi’s death in a helicopter crash in May 2024 prompted an early election, won by Masoud Pezeshkian. Human Rights Watch’s account of that year also documented continuing arrests and restrictions affecting activists, students, and relatives of people killed during the 2022 protests. A change in the presidency therefore needs to be assessed alongside evidence about the conduct of other institutions. [s5]

For 2025, Human Rights Watch described continued persecution of women, minorities, and perceived dissidents. It also reported that the June conflict with Israel was followed by intensified domestic repression justified in the language of national security. This is the organization’s documented assessment; it should not be replaced by an assumption that external conflict suspends domestic political tensions. [s6]

content.heading: A provisional account of developments in 2026
content.content:
The historical account must extend beyond the leadership arrangements familiar from earlier decades. In a report dated 20 March 2026, Associated Press described Ali Khamenei’s death in the opening attacks of the war and the naming of his son Mojtaba as his successor. Its reporting distinguished the successor’s formal position from uncertainty over operational control, including analysts’ assessments of the Revolutionary Guard’s influence. This is a dated account, not verification of the leadership situation in October. [s7]

Separately, the Center for Human Rights in Iran’s September account of the UN fact-finding mission’s latest report described widespread killings, detention, torture, and communications restrictions during the suppression of protests that began in December 2025. It reported the mission’s conclusion that numerous violations amounted to crimes against humanity. The underlying UN report could not be retrieved in this research session; these findings are therefore presented through the inspected secondary account. [s8]

Taken together, the evidence supports reading post-revolutionary politics through both institutions and contested participation. A complete history still requires fuller coverage of the intervening decades and verification of developments through the editorial cutoff.

content.title: Selected relationships in the constitutional text
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Voters"] -->|"Elect the president"| B["President"]
  A -->|"Elect parliamentary representatives"| C["Parliament"]
  D["Leader"] -->|"Appoints clerical members"| E["Guardian Council"]
  C -->|"Sends legislation for review"| E
  E -->|"Reviews compatibility with Islam and constitution"| C
  D -->|"Holds supreme command"| F["Armed forces"]
```
content.summary: This diagram depicts selected relationships in the constitution incorporating the 1989 amendments. It omits many institutions and does not establish how power was exercised in practice or verify the complete legal position in October 2026.
